name: brutalist-design-system

setup.imports: Import every component and block from 'brutalist-design-system'.

layers: Basics (tokens, type, icons, layout) → Components (controls) → Blocks (complete tasks). Compose blocks from components; never restyle a component to change its behaviour.

components.name: NavigationList
components.title: Navigation list
components.useWhen: Users need stable access to pages or major sections of an application.
components.inContext: A workspace sidebar lists Campaigns, Assets, and Settings with one current destination. Project-specific navigation can form a separately labelled group.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use links for destinations and Menu for contextual commands. Use `group` for a concise heading before a new destination section. Use `children` for a disclosure group; if a parent is also a destination, its link stays separate from the disclosure button. Compact rows retain accessible link names and provide tooltips. Use Tabs for peer content panels within one view.
components.behavior: Use clear destination names and one current item per navigation context. Provide real href values and keep selected state synchronized with routing. Icons reinforce labels. Do not rely on a navigation list alone to define page access or enforce permissions.

examples.title: Nested destinations

components.name: NavigationMenu
components.title: Navigation menu
components.useWhen: A page header needs a compact set of primary destinations with one-level grouped links.
components.inContext: An Explore menu opens a short panel of destination links, each with an optional explanatory line.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use `href` for every destination. Use NavigationList for persistent side navigation and Menu for contextual commands. Grouped links stay one level deep so keyboard navigation remains predictable.
components.behavior: Radix owns trigger navigation and Escape behavior. An optional `onNavigate(id)` callback runs on link activation without cancelling native navigation, allowing a surrounding mobile Drawer to close. Provide the Drawer around the navigation at the screen composition level.

examples.title: Destinations and grouped links

components.name: AttachmentArea
components.title: Attachment area
components.useWhen: Files support a primary writing task, such as adding evidence to a note or a document to a prompt.
components.inContext: A reviewer writes a comment, attaches a reference PDF, sees the selected file above the action row, and submits both as one contribution.
components.chooseAndCompose: Compose the editor, file summary, and submit action using shared components. Use FileDropzone when collecting files is the primary task. Do not introduce a second competing upload surface inside the same composer.
components.behavior: Explain file restrictions and preserve the note when attachment selection or submission fails. The application owns the selected-file collection and uploading. Disabling attachment intake does not automatically make all composed child controls read-only; coordinate the state of the entire task.

components.name: Button
components.title: Button
components.useWhen: The user explicitly initiates an operation: create a campaign, save changes, upload a selection, or open a dialog. For navigation to another resource, use a link through TextAction.
components.inContext: A campaign editor ends with a primary “Save changes” button and a secondary “Cancel” action. In a project row, “Duplicate” is a supporting action with less emphasis than the page's main creation action.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use primary emphasis for the main action within a decision area; use neutral or quiet styles for supporting actions. Reserve danger for destructive consequences. A routine “Try again” action is not destructive merely because it follows an error. Use named sizes to match surrounding density, and retain a usable pointer target in compact layouts.
components.behavior: Name the outcome with a verb and object. Explain unavailable actions near the control. While a request is pending, show busy state and prevent duplicate submission; after failure, provide a useful recovery message. Give icon-only buttons an accessible name. Actions use button semantics, while resource navigation uses link semantics. Button pattern, W3C APG

examples.title: Primary (Default)

components.name: Disclosure
components.title: Disclosure
components.useWhen: One named section of supporting content should open in place while the surrounding page remains available.
components.inContext: A record summary reveals its detailed notes beneath a “Collection details” button.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Accordion for several coordinated sections, Dialog for a focused decision, and Disclosure for one independent region. Keep the trigger label specific to the content it reveals.
components.behavior: The consuming page owns controlled open state when needed. Hidden content stays in its associated region and should not contain a duplicate trigger. Disable the trigger only when opening the region is unavailable.

examples.title: Simple
Controlled

components.name: Toolbar
components.title: Toolbar
components.useWhen: Several adjacent commands act on the same content and benefit from one keyboard entry point.
components.inContext: A text editor groups Bold, Copy, and other formatting actions in a labelled command row.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use ButtonGroup for visual grouping without toolbar keyboard navigation. Use ToggleButton alone for one independent pressed action. Choose horizontal or vertical orientation to match the surrounding layout.
components.behavior: Give each command a stable ID and clear name. The application handles onAction and updates pressed items; a controlled pressed value does not change itself. Disabled commands remain unavailable and are skipped during arrow navigation.

examples.title: Horizontal
Vertical

components.name: ToggleButton
components.title: Toggle button
components.useWhen: A single button turns an independent mode on or off.
components.inContext: A view control enables a grid overlay and retains the “Show grid” name as its pressed state changes.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Toggle for a form setting, SegmentedControl for one choice among alternatives, and Toolbar when several commands share an arrow-key group.
components.behavior: Keep the accessible name stable. Use pressed and onPressedChange when the application owns state; use defaultPressed for a local initial state. The application applies the selected mode to the content.

examples.title: Independent

components.name: FeedbackButton
components.title: Feedback button
components.useWhen: A small operation can acknowledge success in the same control, such as copying a code sample or a share link.
components.inContext: “Copy link” changes to “Copied” only after the clipboard operation succeeds. When the underlying link changes, the action becomes available for the new value.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Button with workflow-level feedback for actions that need an ongoing progress view, repeated execution, or a substantial result. FeedbackButton is suited to an operation that completes once for the current content.
components.behavior: Supply an accurate success label and handle failures through the surrounding workflow. The current component suppresses repeat execution after completion until reset; use resetKey when the content or operation identity changes. Do not describe this as an automatically timed confirmation.

components.name: Panel
components.title: Panel
components.useWhen: A coherent set of content and controls needs a named boundary, such as campaign details, an activity summary, or a documentation example.
components.inContext: A “Campaign assets” panel contains filters, the asset list, and actions scoped to that collection. Unrelated account actions live outside the panel.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use split presentation when separating the header from the body clarifies scope. Use compact density for dense operational content. Prefer headings and spacing when a visible frame adds no useful grouping.
components.behavior: Choose the heading level from the page hierarchy. Keep titles descriptive and actions scoped to the panel. Panel is a container, not a clickable card, disclosure, or dialog. Avoid nested panels whose competing borders make relationships harder to read.

components.name: TextField
components.title: Text field
components.useWhen: The user enters a short, single-line value such as a project name, email address, or reference identifier.
components.inContext: “Campaign name” includes a brief naming rule beneath the field. A placeholder can show an example, while the persistent label continues to identify the value after typing.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use TextArea for prose, SearchField for queries, PasswordField for secrets, and a selection control when only predefined values are valid. Use readOnly for a value people should still inspect or copy; disabled means temporarily unavailable.
components.behavior: Match native type and autocomplete to the data. Explain the expected format before submission when it is not obvious. Error text should identify a correction, such as “Enter a work email address,” and remain associated with the field. Avoid errors while the user is still making an ordinary incomplete entry.

components.name: Checkbox
components.title: Checkbox
components.useWhen: Choices are independent: include motion, select several records, or agree to a specific condition before submitting a form.
components.inContext: An export form lets the user choose PDF and PNG independently. In a bulk-action table, a parent checkbox reflects whether none, some, or all rows are selected.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use RadioGroup for exactly one option and Toggle for an immediate on/off setting. Use indeterminate only for a mixed collection state, not as an ambiguous third answer.
components.behavior: State the option positively so checked has a clear meaning. The application must synchronize parent and child selection and define whether select-all affects the current page or all results. Make consent and optional preferences explicit rather than silently preselecting them.

examples.title: Descriptive choice card

components.name: CheckboxCard
components.title: Checkbox card
components.useWhen: An independent choice needs a larger target and one short supporting description.
components.inContext: A delivery form offers an optional printed summary and explains what will be included.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Checkbox for compact choices without supporting detail. Use a RadioCardGroup when only one option may be selected. CheckboxCard remains a native checkbox and submits its normal name/value pair.
components.behavior: Keep the label concise and the description supplementary. The application owns selection state and validation. A read-only choice prevents changes but remains a checkbox; use disabled only when the option is unavailable.

examples.title: Descriptive choice card

components.name: Fieldset
components.title: Fieldset
components.useWhen: Several related native fields need one group name, shared instructions, or shared error context.
components.inContext: Contact preferences sit under one legend, with a short note describing the choice and a group-level validation message.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use a Fieldset for semantic form grouping. Use Panel for a visual content section that is not a form group. Fieldset inherits native disabled behavior for its descendants and does not validate a schema.
components.behavior: Give every group a useful legend. Keep individual field labels and local errors on their controls; group instructions or errors should describe a rule shared by the children.

import 'brutalist-design-system/styles.css'

components.name: RadioGroup
components.title: Radio group
components.useWhen: The user must choose one option and benefits from seeing every alternative at once, such as export orientation or a delivery method.
components.inContext: A format choice shows Square, Portrait, and Landscape together, allowing quick comparison without opening a menu.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Select when the list would occupy too much space, and SegmentedControl for a small immediate mode change such as Grid/List. Use customOption only when a genuine “Other” answer is meaningful and can be handled by the product. Use `variant="tags"` for a short set of choices that reads better as wrapping tags, such as a goal; it keeps radio behaviour, and its custom answer field appears only while that option is selected.
components.behavior: Give the set a question or descriptive label and keep option wording parallel. Explain why a necessary option is unavailable. Choose a default only when it is safe and helpful; do not disguise a required conscious choice with an arbitrary preselection.

examples.title: Plan choice cards

components.name: RadioCardGroup
components.title: Radio cards
components.useWhen: A mutually exclusive choice has a few alternatives that benefit from side-by-side comparison and supporting descriptions.
components.inContext: A workspace selection shows each option's intended audience in addition to its name.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use RadioGroup for brief options without additional detail. Use Select or Combobox when the list is long. RadioCardGroup remains a native radio group with one shared form name and standard arrow-key selection.
components.behavior: Keep descriptions short and distinguish the tradeoffs. The application owns the selected value and validation. Read-only prevents changes while preserving the selected value; disabled means the entire group is unavailable.

examples.title: Plan choice

components.name: Toggle
components.title: Toggle
components.useWhen: A persistent setting can be understood as on or off and takes effect immediately, such as email notifications or a preview mode.
components.inContext: “Email notifications” toggles delivery preferences. If saving fails, the interface restores the previous state and explains the failure beside the setting.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Checkbox when the choice is collected for a later form submission. Use a Button for a one-time command such as sending an email. A potentially destructive operation should not be disguised as a casual preference switch.
components.behavior: Keep the label stable across states and describe the enabled condition. The application owns saving, pending state, rollback, and feedback. Avoid contradictory wording such as an enabled switch labelled “Disable notifications.”

components.name: TextArea
components.title: Text area
components.useWhen: The user writes multiple lines: a campaign brief, comment, rationale, or description.
components.inContext: A brief field explains the information needed—audience, goal, and key message—rather than merely repeating “Enter brief.” Its initial height reflects the expected answer length.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use TextField for short values and InlineText for small edits within existing content. Use embedded presentation only inside another labelled input surface. Choose a dedicated editor when structured rich text is essential.
components.behavior: Explain actual format support and limits. A textarea does not add Markdown rendering or rich-text behavior by itself. Preserve drafts after failures, allow readable wrapping, and keep multiline typing distinct from any submission shortcut supplied by the surrounding workflow.

components.name: Select
components.title: Dropdowns
components.useWhen: A field chooses values from a defined set. Decide first whether the answer is one item or several, and whether users need to search.
components.inContext: A campaign form can use Select for priority, Combobox for one client in a larger directory, and MultiSelect for distribution channels. These are different data questions even though all can reveal choices in a popup.
components.chooseAndCompose: Prefer RadioGroup for a short list that benefits from visible comparison. Use Menu for commands such as duplicate or delete; a command menu does not represent a saved form value. The following three sections belong together on the current combined page but should remain separately identifiable.
components.behavior: Keep the saved value, displayed label, available options, and form submission synchronized. Represent loading, unavailable choices, and no matching results explicitly. Do not use a placeholder as the only field label.

components.name: Tag
components.title: Tag
components.useWhen: An item needs a short label, category, active filter, or workflow state. The plain form is a white tag with a black outline and no icon.
components.inContext: A campaign can have a neutral “Email” category. A filter summary can show a removable “Owner: Mira” tag. A board can use “Planned,” “In progress,” “In review,” “Approved,” and “Blocked” with consistent state treatments.
components.chooseAndCompose: Add an icon when it improves recognition. Use semantic tones for status, not arbitrary decoration. Use a removable variant only when the user can remove that selection or association. A clickable filter choice belongs in a selection control; a tag alone is a label.
components.behavior: Keep the shared 600 text weight and concise wording. Name removal precisely: “Remove owner filter” communicates a different consequence from deleting the person. Reflect the changed selection after removal and preserve a clear empty-filter state.

components.name: TagInput
components.title: Tag input
components.useWhen: People add several short labels to one record, such as topics or skills, and may type new ones.
components.inContext: A note editor lets people add topics; existing topics are suggested while typing and new ones are added with Enter.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Checkbox or MultiSelect when the choices are fixed and known. Keep tags short; long values belong in a list or table.
components.behavior: The application owns the list of values and any suggestions. The input sits after the existing tags. Removing a tag is a named button; duplicates are ignored.

components.name: Breadcrumbs
components.title: Breadcrumbs
components.useWhen: A page belongs to a meaningful hierarchy and users may need to move to its parents.
components.inContext: “Projects / Nordic spring / Brief” shows how the brief relates to its project. Earlier levels link to their destinations; the last label identifies the current page.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use NavigationList for the main application structure and WorkflowSteps for a sequence of tasks. Breadcrumbs describe location, not browser history, completion, or the sequence in which someone happened to open pages.
components.behavior: Keep names consistent with destination headings. Omit meaningless structural levels. Preserve the shared link underline and focus treatment. Long names may wrap or require a deliberate truncation strategy, but users must retain enough context to identify the current item and its parent.

components.name: Pagination
components.title: Pagination
components.useWhen: Users browse a finite result set in pages and benefit from a stable position, such as an audit log or campaign directory.
components.inContext: A result table shows the total count and current page. Moving to another page retains the current filters and sorting.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Pagination when returning to a particular range matters. A small list may need no pagination at all. DotStepper represents position in a short sequence, while WorkflowSteps represents task stages; neither replaces result pagination.
components.behavior: Keep page and page count consistent after filtering or deletion. The application fetches or slices results, handles loading and errors, and manages the URL when needed. Make the new result range discoverable to keyboard and assistive-technology users without unexpectedly moving focus on every update.

components.name: NumberStepper
components.title: Number stepper
components.useWhen: The user adjusts a bounded quantity and often changes it by a small increment, such as copies, seats, or generated variations.
components.inContext: An export configuration offers “Number of variations” with direct numeric entry and increment/decrement controls. It explains any practical limit.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Slider for approximate tuning across a scale, or a plain numeric field when users usually type large, precise values. NumberStepper edits a quantity; WorkflowSteps tracks stages in a process.
components.behavior: State units and choose sensible minimum, maximum, and increment values. Keep the displayed value consistent with the quantity actually submitted. Explain unavailable increments at a domain limit rather than allowing the resulting request to fail without context.

components.name: Slider
components.title: Slider
components.useWhen: Adjusting a value relative to a known range is more important than entering an exact number, such as preview zoom or image quality.
components.inContext: An image editor lets the user tune quality while seeing the result and the current percentage nearby.
components.chooseAndCompose: Set bounds and increments that match the domain. Use NumberStepper or a numeric field for exact quantities, especially when small differences matter. Use RangeSlider for a lower and upper bound together.
components.behavior: Show meaningful units and describe what the ends of the range mean. Preserve keyboard adjustment and keep the numeric value readable. The application decides whether to preview changes immediately or apply them later; expensive processing should not unexpectedly restart on every small movement.

components.name: RangeSlider
components.title: Range slider
components.useWhen: Users define an interval within known bounds, such as a budget or duration filter.
components.inContext: A project search narrows results to budgets between a minimum and maximum amount. Both selected endpoints remain visible with the same unit.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use this for exploratory filtering; provide precise entry when the task depends on exact boundaries. Use separate date fields for calendar intervals. A range slider should not be used to indicate work completed.
components.behavior: Give each endpoint a distinct name and keep lower and upper values ordered. Explain whether the endpoints are inclusive when it matters. The current component coordinates two range inputs; do not promise a single shared-track interaction that the implementation does not provide.

components.name: Rating
components.title: Rating
components.useWhen: Users express a subjective score on a short, ordered scale, such as rating the usefulness of a template after using it.
components.inContext: Ask “How useful was this template?” after the user completes the task, with a consistent five-point scale and an optional explanation field nearby.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use RadioGroup when every option needs a distinct verbal meaning, such as satisfaction levels. Use a numeric field for objective quantities. Avoid using interactive rating controls as an approximate visualization of unrelated metrics.
components.behavior: Explain the scale and how a response is saved. Keep a genuine unanswered state where needed; do not preselect a flattering score. Selectable ratings use whole-number radio choices. Use `readOnly` to present a supplied value, including a fractional average; it displays the numeric text and decorative stars without radio controls. It does not provide half-step interaction.

components.name: ProgressBar
components.title: Progress bar
components.useWhen: The user is waiting for work with measurable completion, such as uploading files, generating assets, or exporting a report. The horizontal form leaves room for a task label and useful detail.
components.inContext: An export panel shows “Exporting 12 assets” and progress based on completed work. After processing finishes, it replaces the progress state with a download action or a recoverable error.
components.chooseAndCompose: Supply a value and maximum when completion is known. Omit the value for indeterminate work; never simulate accuracy with an invented percentage. Use WorkflowSteps for named stages, Spinner for a small unknown wait, and ProgressRing for compact completion summaries. Static storage capacity is a meter use case, not task progress.
components.behavior: Label the operation and explain the measure when necessary: files processed is not elapsed time remaining. Keep long-running work close to relevant cancel or retry actions. Reaching 100% must not imply success while another stage can still fail. Provide a final outcome separately.

components.name: ProgressRing
components.title: Progress ring
components.useWhen: A compact, known completion ratio belongs beside a named task or summary, such as “8 of 10 onboarding tasks complete.”
components.inContext: An onboarding summary places the ring next to its title and a description explaining what remains. Users open a stepper or checklist to see the individual requirements.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use ProgressBar for a long-running operation whose detail deserves a row. Use a stepper when sequence matters. The current ring requires a value; use Spinner for unknown progress. Avoid repeated rings when users primarily need to compare exact values across many records.
components.behavior: Include a meaningful label and denominator or explanatory description. Do not equate checklist completion with time remaining. Although a ring can visually resemble a capacity gauge, this component exposes progressbar semantics; use Meter for static quota or capacity readings.

components.name: DescriptionList
components.title: Description list
components.useWhen: Several related terms need their corresponding descriptions without a repeated table header.
components.inContext: A record summary pairs “Owner” with a person, “Status” with its current state, and “Updated” with a date.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use stacked details for a short single-column summary and columns when related pairs benefit from side-by-side scanning. Use Table when people compare repeated records by shared fields.
components.behavior: Supply stable item IDs and meaningful terms. Keep long values readable as they wrap, and do not assume that the list sorts, edits, or fetches its values.

examples.title: Stacked details
Columns and long values

components.name: Stat
components.title: Stat
components.useWhen: A single measured value needs a clear label and enough context to interpret it.
components.inContext: A service summary shows “18 requests” over “the last 24 hours,” with a separately supplied comparison to the previous period.
components.chooseAndCompose: Keep the unit, denominator, time period, and data source near the value when they affect its meaning. Use Table or DescriptionList for a set of distinct facts.
components.behavior: Zero is a valid value. Use `null` with an explicit unavailable label when no value exists. Comparison text and direction are supplied by the application; the component does not decide whether an increase is desirable.

import 'brutalist-design-system/styles.css'

export function ComparisonExample() {

components.name: Timeline
components.title: Timeline
components.useWhen: People need to follow a supplied sequence of dated events.
components.inContext: A document history shows when a brief was created, reviewed, and approved, with an optional link to the related review.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use WorkflowSteps for a named process with a current step. Use a table when users need to compare many independent events across common columns.
components.behavior: Supply items in the intended reading order with stable IDs, machine-readable `dateTime` values, and visible date labels. The application owns event creation, ordering, and action behavior.

examples.title: Dated history

components.name: Meter
components.title: Meter
components.useWhen: A value describes a bounded measurement such as quota, storage, or capacity.
components.inContext: A settings summary shows three gigabytes used out of ten and includes that unit in the accessible value text.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use ProgressBar or ProgressRing for work moving toward completion. Use a plain Stat when an indicator adds no useful information beyond the value and unit.
components.behavior: Provide meaningful bounds and an accessible label. Use `valueText` when a raw number lacks useful units. Thresholds describe the measurement's range and are not completion states.

components.name: SectionHeading
components.title: Section heading
components.useWhen: A content section needs a consistent heading, optional context, and optional adjacent actions.
components.inContext: A history section places “Recent activity” and a short explanation beside a link to the complete history.
components.chooseAndCompose: Select the semantic heading level from the page outline. Use Heading directly when no shared title and actions layout is needed.
components.behavior: Keep the title specific to its section and choose heading level independently from visual type style. Actions remain the caller's responsibility and wrap when space is limited.

examples.title: Description and action
Wrapped actions

components.name: PasswordStrength
components.title: Password requirements
components.useWhen: A form needs to show which supplied password requirements have been met.
components.inContext: An account form lists minimum length and uniqueness requirements beside the password field as the person types.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use inline field instructions for static guidance that has no changing requirement states. Use this checklist only when the application can provide each current met state.
components.behavior: Supply labels and boolean states for stable requirement IDs. The component presents these values; the application owns password validation and security policy. Do not expose the password value or imply a strength score unless the product has a defined scoring method.

examples.title: Mixed requirements
Requirements met

components.name: Alert
components.title: Alert
components.useWhen: An important message belongs beside the content it explains: a validation summary, a delayed export, a save result, or a condition that changes the user's next step.
components.inContext: An import form shows “Two columns need mapping” directly above the affected controls and offers “Review columns.” A completed save can show a quieter confirmation in the same area.
components.chooseAndCompose: Choose tone by meaning and surface strength by prominence. Filled treatment suits an exceptional message requiring attention; light and stroke treatments integrate with ordinary content. A larger variant suits a message with explanation and an action. Use Banner for workspace-wide conditions, Toast for brief feedback, and Dialog when a response is required before proceeding.
components.behavior: Explain what happened and what can be done. Use `announcement="polite"` or `"assertive"` deliberately for newly appearing important messages; `off` removes live announcement semantics when another mechanism already communicates the update. The legacy `announce` boolean remains supported. Do not repeatedly announce every render. An alert should not take keyboard focus simply to be noticed. Alert pattern, W3C APG

components.name: InlineText
components.title: Text with inline editing
components.useWhen: A small, existing value can be edited directly in its context, such as renaming a project or adjusting a short description.
components.inContext: A project title becomes editable without opening a separate settings page. Saving updates the title; failure leaves the draft available for correction or retry.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use a Form for several dependent fields and TextArea for substantial writing. Avoid immediate inline saving for changes whose consequences require review before committing.
components.behavior: Make editability discoverable and label the editable value. Enter saves, Shift+Enter inserts a line, Escape cancels, and blur attempts to save. Explain this when unfamiliar users could lose their place. The application owns persistence and must not report success before saving completes.

components.name: TextAction
components.title: Text action
components.useWhen: Navigation or a secondary action should sit comfortably within prose, metadata, or a compact message. Examples include “View invoice,” “Read the guide,” and “Clear filters.”
components.inContext: An export notification offers “View export details” as a link. A search summary offers “Clear filters” as a button styled with the same low emphasis.
components.chooseAndCompose: Provide href for a destination; use the action form for changes in the current interface. Use a regular Button when the task is the primary decision or needs a stronger visual target.
components.behavior: Write a label that identifies the destination or effect without surrounding text. Avoid repeated “Click here” links. Underlining must remain recognizable, and keyboard focus must be visible. Explain unavailable navigation in the surrounding UI rather than assuming a link supports the same disabled behavior as a button.

components.name: Form
components.title: Form
components.useWhen: Related inputs contribute to one submission, such as creating a workspace or saving campaign settings.
components.inContext: A campaign form groups its title, launch date, and distribution settings, then ends with FormActions. Each field explains its own constraints.
components.chooseAndCompose: Group fields by the user's mental model and place dependent questions after the choice that reveals them. Use a multi-step workflow only when task complexity justifies dividing the work. Do not wrap every independent immediate setting in a large save form.
components.behavior: Give the form a meaningful name. Define submission, validation, and persistence in the application; Form supplies structure rather than a form-state engine. Preserve values on failure and make invalid fields easy to find. Avoid nested forms.

components.name: FormActions
components.title: Form actions
components.useWhen: A form has one submission point and an optional way to abandon changes. Use it for account settings, a new project form, or editing a contact.
components.inContext: After campaign settings, “Save changes” commits the whole form and “Cancel” returns to the previous state. A nearby message confirms the completed save or explains what still needs attention.
components.chooseAndCompose: Put this row at the end of Form, close enough that its scope is clear. Use a specific submit label such as “Create project.” For immediate per-field updates, provide feedback beside the changed field instead of implying that another save is required.
components.behavior: The application owns submission, cancellation, validation, and dirty-state handling. Use busy during submission and preserve entered values on failure. Ensure the user can find invalid fields; a status message beneath the buttons should not be the only explanation.

components.name: SearchField
components.title: Search field
components.useWhen: A query narrows or locates content, such as campaigns, people, files, or documentation pages.
components.inContext: “Search campaigns” sits above the campaign results. Clearing it restores the unfiltered results while preserving unrelated filter selections.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Combobox when the result is one selected value, and CommandMenu when the result is an action. Keep search scope explicit; a search of the current project should not imply a workspace-wide search.
components.behavior: Choose whether results update while typing or on submission, and make that behavior consistent. The application owns filtering, request timing, stale responses, result count, and empty results. Preserve the query during navigation when that helps users return to their work.

components.name: PasswordField
components.title: Password field
components.useWhen: The user enters a secret, such as a sign-in password or a replacement password in account settings.
components.inContext: A new-password field explains requirements before entry and allows the user to reveal the value while checking it. A sign-in field supports the browser's existing-password autofill.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use appropriate autocomplete for current versus new passwords. Do not substitute DigitInput for an ordinary password or block paste and password-manager entry.
components.behavior: Keep the visible label and validation message clear. The application handles authentication and saving; the field's visibility toggle only changes local presentation. Avoid exposing the secret in confirmation text, notifications, or error messages.

components.name: DatePicker
components.title: Date picker
components.useWhen: A user chooses a calendar date, such as a launch day, due date, or reporting cutoff.
components.inContext: A launch-date field limits selection to dates permitted by the campaign schedule and explains the earliest allowed day.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use explicit date fields for precise calendar choices. A relative preset such as “Last 7 days” may suit a reporting filter better, but requires separate product logic. Do not imply that a single date field supports ranges, recurring schedules, or time selection.
components.behavior: Explain constraints beside the field. Keep date-only values distinct from timestamps so timezone conversion does not shift the chosen calendar day. The application owns scheduling rules and validation against other fields; a selected date alone does not schedule work.

components.name: Calendar
components.title: Calendar
components.useWhen: A date must be picked in context and the calendar should stay visible, such as a booking sidebar.
components.inContext: A booking page shows the month with unavailable days disabled, so people can see what is free before choosing.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use DatePicker when the calendar should appear only on demand next to a field; use DateRangePicker for a start and end.
components.behavior: Arrow keys move between days; Page Up and Page Down change month. Values are ISO calendar dates without time zone conversion; the application decides which days are available.

components.name: DateRangePicker
components.title: Date range picker
components.useWhen: People choose a start and an end date for a report, a stay or a filter.
components.inContext: A report filter offers a range field; the calendar opens in a popup and Today and Clear sit beside the months.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use DatePicker for one date. Use a SegmentedControl of presets (7, 30, 90 days) when exact dates rarely matter, and keep the range field as the precise option.
components.behavior: The end cannot come before the start. Values are ISO dates; the application validates business rules such as a maximum span and applies the filter.

examples.title: Editable period

components.name: TimeField
components.title: Time field
components.useWhen: People enter a local time of day, such as a reminder or opening hours.
components.inContext: A reminder form pairs a DatePicker with a TimeField and shows common times in a popup.
components.chooseAndCompose: Pair with DatePicker for a moment in time. Do not use it for durations; use NumberStepper with a unit instead.
components.behavior: Values are local HH:mm with no implicit time zone. Typed and chosen times produce the same value; invalid input shows an error linked to the field.
components.props: export type TimeFieldProps = Omit<TextFieldProps, 'type'>;

examples.title: Native time input

components.name: Menu
components.title: Menu
components.useWhen: An object has several contextual commands that do not all need permanent visibility, such as Edit, Duplicate, Download, and Delete.
components.inContext: A campaign row has a “More campaign actions” trigger. Frequent primary work remains visible; less common commands are available in the menu.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Select for choosing a saved value and NavigationList for normal navigation. Use ButtonGroup when a few related actions deserve to remain visible. The current menu is a flat command list, not a nested application menubar.
components.behavior: Use verb-led item labels and mark destructive consequences clearly. An icon-only trigger still needs an accessible name identifying its scope. Explain unavailable capabilities where users can discover the reason. Menu groups and separators are structural labels, not focusable items. Links retain native destinations; disabled links have no destination. Checkbox and radio values remain controlled by the consumer; selections stay open, while ordinary commands and links close the menu. Selecting a destructive command may open a separate confirmation; opening the menu must not execute it.

examples.title: Grouped selections and links

components.name: Dialog
components.title: Dialog
components.useWhen: A focused decision or short task needs to temporarily interrupt the current flow, such as confirming workspace deletion or editing a small set of critical details.
components.inContext: Before deleting a workspace, the dialog names it, explains the consequence, and gives explicit cancel and delete actions.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use InlineConfirmation for a short localized confirmation, Popover for contextual controls, and a dedicated page for long tasks or extensive content. Avoid opening modal dialogs for routine success messages.
components.behavior: Make the title and action labels explain the decision. Preserve a clear close or cancel path, meaningful focus on opening, and a sensible return destination on closing. Use a focusable, accessibly named `triggerElement` when the default trigger does not fit the layout. A triggerless dialog requires controlled `open` state, `onOpenChange`, and an explicit `returnFocusRef`. Set `dismissible={false}` only when dismissal is unsafe; Escape, outside interaction, and the close control are then blocked. The application owns submission and whether successful completion closes the dialog. Resolve unsaved work intentionally and avoid nested dialogs where a single clear task is possible.

components.name: Drawer
components.title: Drawer
components.useWhen: Supporting navigation or a focused detail task can enter from the edge while retaining visual context of the underlying page.
components.inContext: On a narrow viewport, a navigation drawer exposes workspace destinations. In an operational view, a drawer may present a short record-editing task.
components.chooseAndCompose: The current Drawer is modal: background content is not simultaneously interactive. If users must compare and edit the underlying page at the same time, use a persistent panel or a dedicated split layout. Use Dialog for a compact central decision.
components.behavior: Provide a clear title and close action. Preserve readable content, reachable actions, and appropriate scrolling on small screens. The application owns draft retention and any warning before closing with unsaved changes. Do not choose a drawer simply to avoid deciding where a complex feature belongs.

components.name: Popover
components.title: Popover
components.useWhen: A small amount of contextual content or a few controls should appear near their trigger, such as display options or a compact filter panel.
components.inContext: An asset view opens display preferences beside the view controls, allowing the user to adjust local presentation without leaving the collection.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Tooltip for a brief optional explanation, Menu for a list of commands, and Dialog for a substantial task or consequential decision. Use the field-like trigger only when it represents a field interaction in the surrounding composition.
components.behavior: Name the trigger by what will open. A custom `triggerElement` must remain focusable and accessibly named. Keep the content short enough to remain usable within the viewport. Define whether changes apply immediately or require an explicit action, and keep closing behavior from silently discarding substantial work. Preserve keyboard access to both trigger and contents.

components.name: Tooltip
components.title: Tooltip
components.useWhen: A short, optional explanation helps users understand a term or control without expanding the whole page.
components.inContext: Beside an export setting, a help trigger explains how the setting affects image quality. The setting's name and required instructions remain visible without opening the tooltip.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Hint for field requirements and persistent instructions. Use Popover for links, controls, or longer contextual information. A tooltip should not contain a form, a decision, or the only explanation of an error.
components.behavior: Write one concise thought and avoid repeating the trigger label. Ensure equivalent help is available to touch users when it is necessary to complete the task. The default trigger is a labelled help button; a custom `triggerElement` must preserve an accessible name and keyboard focus.

examples.title: Custom trigger

components.name: Toast
components.title: Toast
components.useWhen: Brief feedback confirms an action without interrupting the current activity, such as saving a draft or changing a setting.
components.inContext: After a successful rename, “Project renamed” confirms the result while the updated title remains visible. Failure to rename also needs a recovery path near the editable title.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use FeedbackButton for a small action whose confirmation fits inside the control. Use Alert or Notification when information must remain available or requires a follow-up decision. Avoid making a toast the only place to discover a failed submission.
components.behavior: Keep messages concise and avoid repeated announcements for the same event. The default announcement is polite, with danger or warning tones announced assertively; set `announcement` to `off`, `polite`, or `assertive` to control this. The component provides one live region and dismissal but does not schedule its own expiry or manage a queue. If the application adds timed dismissal, essential information and actions must remain accessible through a persistent surface.

components.name: Tabs
components.title: Tabs
components.useWhen: Peer content sections share one context and the user benefits from switching between them, such as Overview, Activity, and Files within a project.
components.inContext: The project header remains stable while the selected tab changes the content panel. The tab names tell users where to find information without opening every panel.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use SegmentedControl for modes of the same content and NavigationList for distinct destinations in the application. Choose compact tabs when the surrounding content is dense. Vertical orientation suits settings areas with longer section names. Keep content-panel tabs distinct from the component's compatibility support for segmented options.
components.behavior: Preserve relevant work when switching, make selection clear, and connect tabs to their panels. If a view needs a shareable URL, the application must synchronize it. Tab semantics describe layered content panels rather than arbitrary navigation. Tabs pattern, W3C APG

examples.title: Vertical tabs

components.name: WorkflowSteps
components.title: Workflow steps
components.useWhen: A process has named stages and users need to understand both position and completion, such as Brief, Review, and Publish.
components.inContext: Campaign setup shows the current stage, permits returning to completed work, and makes Publish unavailable until required checks are satisfied.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use horizontal orientation for a short sequence with concise labels. Choose vertical orientation or VerticalStepper for longer explanations. Use ProgressBar for measurable background work and Tabs for sections that have no progression or completion relationship. NumberStepper changes a quantity and serves a different task.
components.behavior: Keep current, complete, and disabled states distinct. Supply completion from valid application data, not from visiting a stage. Set `readOnly` or omit `onChange` for a static sequence with no inert buttons; `disabled` keeps transitions visible but unavailable. The application owns validation and transition rules. Keep descriptions under their headings and marker alignment consistent, so one longer description does not suggest a different stage hierarchy.

components.name: Table
components.title: Table
components.useWhen: Users compare records across the same attributes, such as project name, owner, status, and last update.
components.inContext: An operations view uses sortable project rows to find recent work. Row actions remain separate from the data, and a nearby result count explains the scope of the table.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use a list or cards when each item has substantially different content or visual scanning is more important than column comparison. Keep column labels and units consistent. Place filters and Pagination around the table when needed.
components.behavior: The application must actually reorder or refetch rows when sort changes; a sort indicator alone is insufficient. Preserve stable row identity. Optional selection is controlled by selectedIds and reports changes; select-all applies to selectable rows on the current page while retaining IDs from other pages. Use loading and error states to distinguish pending data from an empty result. On narrow screens, retain readable content through the shared scroll region rather than compressing everything.

components.name: Combobox
components.title: Dropdowns
components.useWhen: A field chooses values from a defined set. Decide first whether the answer is one item or several, and whether users need to search.
components.inContext: A campaign form can use Select for priority, Combobox for one client in a larger directory, and MultiSelect for distribution channels. These are different data questions even though all can reveal choices in a popup.
components.chooseAndCompose: Prefer RadioGroup for a short list that benefits from visible comparison. Use Menu for commands such as duplicate or delete; a command menu does not represent a saved form value. The following three sections belong together on the current combined page but should remain separately identifiable.
components.behavior: Keep the saved value, displayed label, available options, and form submission synchronized. Represent loading, unavailable choices, and no matching results explicitly. Do not use a placeholder as the only field label.

components.name: MultiSelect
components.title: Dropdowns
components.useWhen: A field chooses values from a defined set. Decide first whether the answer is one item or several, and whether users need to search.
components.inContext: A campaign form can use Select for priority, Combobox for one client in a larger directory, and MultiSelect for distribution channels. These are different data questions even though all can reveal choices in a popup.
components.chooseAndCompose: Prefer RadioGroup for a short list that benefits from visible comparison. Use Menu for commands such as duplicate or delete; a command menu does not represent a saved form value. The following three sections belong together on the current combined page but should remain separately identifiable.
components.behavior: Keep the saved value, displayed label, available options, and form submission synchronized. Represent loading, unavailable choices, and no matching results explicitly. Do not use a placeholder as the only field label.

components.name: InlineConfirmation
components.title: Inline confirmation
components.useWhen: A localized destructive action needs one short confirmation while its target remains visible, such as deleting a draft from a row.
components.inContext: “Delete draft” expands beside the named draft to explain that the draft will be removed. Cancel restores the original row without changing the data.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Dialog when the consequences involve multiple objects, substantial explanation, or another required decision. Prefer a recoverable action with undo where that is appropriate to the product. Avoid confirmation for routine, harmless operations.
components.behavior: Name the affected object and consequence in the question. Keep failure feedback beside the decision and allow retry. The confirming button repeats the trigger label by default; pass `confirmLabel` for a more specific verb and `tone="neutral"` when the action is consequential but not destructive.

components.name: FileDropzone
components.title: File dropzone
components.useWhen: Selecting one or more files is a main step, such as importing a contact list or uploading campaign assets.
components.inContext: An import panel explains accepted formats and per-file limits before selection. Chosen files appear in FileList; actual upload state replaces idle instructions during transfer.
components.chooseAndCompose: Keep the file-picker button available alongside drag and drop. Use AttachmentArea for optional files accompanying a note. Use meaningful state feedback for uploading, completed, and failed work.
components.behavior: FileDropzone selects and checks files locally; the application performs the upload, repeats validation at the receiving service, and supplies progress and recovery. A null progress value indicates unknown progress and uses an indeterminate bar. A rejected batch stays intact; onReject identifies each rejected file and its type, size, or count reason. Display only measured progress and make recovery actions clear.

examples.title: Validation and upload progress

components.name: FileList
components.title: File list
components.useWhen: Users need to review files selected for a task or already associated with a record.
components.inContext: Below an upload area, a list shows filenames and sizes so users can catch an accidental selection before submitting.
components.chooseAndCompose: Add removal only when it has a defined meaning. Removing a pending attachment is different from deleting an uploaded file for everyone. Use a richer table when users need to compare dates, owners, versions, or transfer status.
components.behavior: Keep filenames legible and identify each action with its file. FileItem status can represent queued, uploading, complete, and error states; uploading with omitted progress is indeterminate. Provide onCancel for queued or active uploads and onRetry for errors. Removal, persistence, downloads, previews, and storage deletion remain application responsibilities.

examples.title: Upload states and actions

export function ListExample() {
  return <FileList files={[
