}

components.name: EmptyState
components.title: Empty state
components.useWhen: A collection or workspace has no content to show and the reason or next step needs explanation.
components.inContext: A first-use campaign list says “No campaigns yet” and offers “Create campaign.” A filtered list says “No campaigns match these filters” and offers “Clear filters.”
components.chooseAndCompose: Tailor the message to first use, no search matches, unavailable access, or a legitimately empty result. Use Alert for a failed load rather than implying the collection is empty. Place the empty state in the region where results would normally appear.
components.behavior: Offer an action the current user can actually perform. Avoid repeated onboarding instructions for experienced users viewing a narrow filter. Keep the title specific and the description focused on how to proceed.

components.name: Spinner
components.title: Spinner
components.useWhen: An operation is running but its completion cannot be measured, and the surrounding area can remain compact.
components.inContext: “Loading preview” appears in the preview region while an asset is fetched. The editor around it can stay usable if that operation does not block editing.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Button's busy state for an action already represented by a button. Use Skeleton when the future content shape is predictable. Use ProgressBar when measurable progress is available.
components.behavior: Name the actual operation. Replace the spinner with content, an empty state, or a recoverable error when work ends. Do not leave an indefinite spinner after a failed request or cover unrelated controls merely because one region is loading.

components.name: Skeleton
components.title: Skeleton
components.useWhen: Text-like content is loading and preserving its approximate space makes the page easier to follow.
components.inContext: A details panel reserves several lines while its description loads, preventing surrounding content from jumping when the response arrives.
components.chooseAndCompose: Match the placeholder's extent to the expected content. The current component provides placeholder lines; it is not a general builder for avatars, charts, or every possible card shape. Use Spinner when no meaningful content shape is known.
components.behavior: Identify the loading region and remove the placeholder when the request resolves. Empty responses need an empty state, and failures need an error explanation. Avoid showing a new skeleton over readable content during a minor refresh when that content can remain useful.

components.name: ButtonGroup
components.title: Button group
components.useWhen: Several actions operate on the same object and should be understood together. Examples include “Save / Save as draft / More,” or “Download PDF / Download CSV.”
components.inContext: In a report header, show the common export action beside a Menu for less frequent export commands. Keep the group near the report it affects. A separate destructive action should not look like an equally safe continuation of the main task.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use attached buttons when the actions form one compact unit; use separated buttons when their boundaries need more emphasis. Assign importance and color to each child according to its consequence. For Grid/List selection, use SegmentedControl; for content sections, use Tabs. A text editor's Bold/Italic commands may be grouped, but each independent toggle needs its own pressed state and the editor must own formatting behavior.
components.behavior: Grouping does not create selection state, mutual exclusivity, split-button behavior, or toolbar keyboard navigation. Keep every child individually named and operable. If a group becomes crowded, promote frequent actions and move secondary commands into Menu. Do not shrink labels until the choices become ambiguous.

components.name: FancyButton
components.title: Fancy button
components.useWhen: One action needs a short supporting line before the user can confidently choose it. This is useful for starting setup, opening a workspace chooser, or beginning an import with a meaningful consequence.
components.inContext: “Import contacts” can have the subtitle “Review a CSV before adding people.” The second line tells the user what will happen next; it should not repeat “Import contacts.”
components.chooseAndCompose: Use a regular Button when its label fully explains the action. Keep FancyButton for occasional, prominent decisions rather than repeated table actions. A choice among plans with prices and features needs a richer selection pattern.
components.behavior: Keep the title action-led and the subtitle brief. Preserve the shared spacing between text and icon, and allow wrapping without clipping. A trailing arrow does not change the control into a link; use link semantics when the operation is purely navigation.

components.name: Avatar
components.title: Avatar
components.useWhen: Recognizing a person helps the user scan ownership, comments, activity, or assignments.
components.inContext: Show an avatar beside the author's name in a comment, or beside the assignee in a task row. In an unfamiliar team, the visible name matters more than the portrait alone.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use the shared circular sizes and match neighboring controls. Initials cover people without a supplied image. Show presence only when the application has trustworthy, current presence data; online status is different from permission or task completion.
components.behavior: Supply a meaningful name even when an image exists. Keep people identifiable without relying on portrait recognition or color. Failed images fall back to initials. Avatar itself is an identity marker, so provide a separate accessible action if users can open a profile.

examples.title: Image fallback

components.name: AvatarGroup
components.title: Avatar group
components.useWhen: A small collection of people can be summarized visually, such as project collaborators or assigned reviewers.
components.inContext: A project header shows a few collaborators and an overflow count, with an explicit “View members” action nearby. The full member list supplies names, roles, and any management actions.
components.chooseAndCompose: Keep all avatars in one group at the same size. Set the visible limit to fit the context without making overlap obscure identity. Use a named list when the user needs to compare or select individuals.
components.behavior: Give the group a contextual label such as “Project reviewers.” The overflow count indicates hidden members; it is not an automatic expandable control. Provide access to the full list and do not imply the order represents rank unless that meaning is explicit.

components.name: Badge
components.title: Badge
components.useWhen: A brief, non-interactive annotation helps users scan a record: “New,” “Beta,” “Approved,” or a plan category.
components.inContext: A feature name may carry a “Beta” badge, or a table row may show an approval state. The surrounding text identifies what the badge qualifies.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use a neutral tone for categories, and semantic color only when the label describes a meaningful state. Use Tag for editable metadata or removable selections. Use StatusBadge when the shared status mapping fits the product's vocabulary.
components.behavior: Keep labels concise and understandable without their color. Badges are not buttons or filters. If the label becomes an action, choose a control with matching interaction semantics. Do not alternate Badge and Tag for the same status merely for visual variety.

components.name: Banner
components.title: Banner
components.useWhen: A condition affects the whole workspace or a substantial area of the current task, such as maintenance, read-only mode, or an integration outage.
components.inContext: Place a maintenance banner above the workspace content so users see it before attempting edits. Its message explains the impact, and a short “Details” action provides further context.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Alert for a problem confined to one form or panel. Use Notification for an event such as a completed export. Keep workspace banners scarce and prioritize overlapping messages.
components.behavior: State the condition, user impact, and useful next step. Offer dismissal only when hiding the message will not make the current state misleading, and set `dismissLabel` when “Dismiss” needs more context. The default `announcement="polite"` preserves the current status announcement; use `off` for messages already covered by a separately announced summary, or `assertive` for urgent content. The application decides how long dismissal lasts and when the banner returns.

components.name: Kbd
components.title: Kbd
components.useWhen: A real keyboard shortcut can speed up an action users already understand.
components.inContext: A command launcher can show the supported shortcut next to “Search commands.” A save action can advertise its shortcut without requiring the user to memorize it.
components.chooseAndCompose: Keep the ordinary clickable action available. Display platform-appropriate modifiers and key names. Place the shortcut beside its action, not as an unexplained string of symbols.
components.behavior: Kbd styles key names; it does not register a keyboard handler. Only advertise shortcuts that the application implements. Avoid intercepting typing or established browser commands unexpectedly, and describe combinations clearly enough to be understood when read aloud.

components.name: ColorPicker
components.title: Color picker
components.useWhen: Choosing an actual color is part of the user's work, such as configuring a brand accent or editing a visual asset.
components.inContext: A brand settings panel provides common presets and a visible hex value that can be copied from an existing brand specification.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use named semantic styles when users are assigning meaning, such as task status, rather than asking them to invent colors for that meaning. The current picker supports solid hex colors; gradients and opacity are separate capabilities.
components.behavior: Keep the exact value visible and validate manual entry. Show the effect of the choice in its real context. The application must preserve readable text and focus states when the selected color affects controls; selecting a color does not certify its contrast.

components.name: DigitInput
components.title: Digit input
components.useWhen: A short, fixed-length numeric code benefits from separated positions, such as a verification code.
components.inContext: A verification step identifies where the code was sent, displays the expected number of cells, and keeps resend and correction guidance nearby.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use a normal field for variable-length identifiers, phone numbers, or alphanumeric codes. DigitInput renders a separately labelled native input for each position, while its controlled value remains one string. Typing advances between positions; arrow keys and Backspace support correction. The first position receives one-time-code autofill, and pasting distributes digits across the remaining positions.
components.behavior: Use a string so leading zeros retain meaning. When `name` is supplied, the form submits one hidden concatenated value rather than a separate field per position. The control filters non-digits, truncates to the configured length, and supports required, readOnly, disabled, and described error states. Keep expiry, resend, submission, and server validation in the application. Preserve usable cell widths and a layout that fits narrow screens.

examples.title: Verification code

components.name: Hint
components.title: Hint
components.useWhen: A field needs short, persistent guidance or a nearby correction message.
components.inContext: Under a project slug, show “Use lowercase letters and hyphens.” After invalid input, explain exactly what needs to change.
components.chooseAndCompose: Prefer a field's instructions and error props when available, since they keep support text attached to the correct control. Use Hint for custom compositions. Use Tooltip only for optional supplementary explanation.
components.behavior: Answer a likely question rather than restating the label. Associate standalone support text with the control and keep it available while typing. Danger styling alone does not connect a message to a field or announce it; the composed control must supply the appropriate relationship.

components.name: Label
components.title: Label
components.useWhen: A standalone input needs a persistent visible name. Prefer the built-in label prop when the shared field already provides one.
components.inContext: A composed settings control has the label “Workspace name,” a separate instruction about naming rules, and an input connected to that label.
components.chooseAndCompose: Labels identify the value; Hint explains constraints. Placeholder examples supplement both. Keep labels brief and use consistent terminology across summaries, forms, and errors.
components.behavior: Associate standalone labels with their input. A visible required marker communicates a requirement but does not enforce it; set the corresponding input behavior and validation. Avoid adding a second visible label around a component that already renders its own.

components.name: Accordion
components.title: Accordion
components.useWhen: Users need to inspect selected sections of related information without reading every section at once, such as FAQs or optional configuration details.
components.inContext: An export help area exposes topic summaries and expands the relevant explanation in place. Multiple-open mode lets users compare two answers.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use single-open behavior for focused inspection and multiple-open behavior when comparison matters. Use normal headings for content everyone must read, and Tabs for distinct peer views. Avoid hiding required form fields or blocking errors inside an unexplained collapsed section.
components.behavior: Write summaries that predict the content. Keep the right-side affordance aligned with the heading, preserve readable body text, and accommodate long answers. Opening a section should not unexpectedly jump the user to another location. Respect reduced-motion preferences for expansion transitions.

components.name: DotStepper
components.title: Dot stepper
components.useWhen: A short, low-complexity sequence needs a compact position indicator and the current screen already explains the content.
components.inContext: A short optional introduction shows which screen is active while its heading supplies the topic. Visible next/back actions remain available.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use a labelled stepper for processes where stage names, requirements, or errors matter. Avoid dots for long workflows or for navigating an arbitrary number of result pages.
components.behavior: Give every position a meaningful accessible name and keep selection synchronized with the displayed screen. Dots are buttons only when `onChange` is provided; omit it or set `readOnly` for static progress, and use `disabled` when transitions are unavailable. Do not imply independent completion states: earlier-dot completion is derived from `current` for backward compatibility.

components.name: VerticalStepper
components.title: Vertical stepper
components.useWhen: A staged process needs persistent names and, when useful, explanations alongside the work. Typical contexts are onboarding, setup, and review preparation.
components.inContext: A workspace setup flow lists Create account, Review details, and Finish setup. The description variant tells users what each stage requires; the header-only variant suits returning users who already understand the process.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use descriptions when stage names alone cannot explain the task. Keep headers only when the sequence is clear. Use per-step `disabled` when a future step must not be opened yet. Use a checklist for tasks that can be completed independently without a meaningful order.
components.behavior: Store current stage and completion separately. Preserve data when users return to earlier stages. A static stepper has no step buttons; interactive use requires `onChange`, and per-step `disabled` prevents that transition. Do not treat visual state as a substitute for application validation.

components.name: CommandMenu
components.title: Command menu
components.useWhen: Experienced users benefit from searching a set of application actions, such as creating a project or opening settings.
components.inContext: A visible “Search commands” launcher supplements normal navigation. Typing narrows the available commands, and selecting one runs the identified action.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Menu for a short object-specific action list, SearchField for searching content, and Combobox for selecting a field value. Keep core tasks discoverable through the ordinary interface so the command menu remains an accelerator.
components.behavior: Use distinct action names and expose only actions appropriate to the current context. Search includes each command's label and optional keywords. Group labels are descriptive only; arrows, Home, and End navigate enabled actions, and Enter runs the active action. Escape closes the dialog and restores trigger focus. Register the optional `mod+k` shortcut only when requested, and keep it out of editable targets.

examples.title: Searchable actions

components.name: NotificationList
components.title: Notification list
components.useWhen: A popover or panel shows a short feed of recent events: who or what, the message and when.
components.inContext: A header bell opens a popover with unread events in bold, a count beside the heading and a Mark all read action.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Toast for one transient confirmation and Alert for a message that belongs in the page flow. Use an avatar for events caused by a person and an icon for system events.
components.behavior: The application owns the items, read state and links. Keep each message to one sentence; put dates in detail and relative time in time. Linked rows are ordinary links.

components.name: StatCard
components.title: Stat card
components.useWhen: A single figure needs its label, change against a period and an optional icon, as a card on its own.
components.inContext: An overview row shows revenue, orders and conversion, each with the change against the previous period.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Figure inside a Tile when the figure shares a tile with a chart. Use Stat inside other content.
components.behavior: Show the period the change compares against. Direction is shown by an arrow and words, never colour alone.

components.name: Sparkline
components.title: Sparkline
components.useWhen: A trend matters more than exact values, beside a figure or in a small tile.
components.inContext: A payouts tile shows the last twelve weeks as a thin line under the headline amount.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use LineChart when people need axes, exact values or several series.
components.behavior: Give it a label that names the period. It has no table view; state the key value in text nearby.

components.name: LineChart
components.title: Line chart
components.useWhen: People compare a value over time, for one to three series.
components.inContext: A revenue tile shows monthly revenue since April with a Weekly or Monthly switch.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use BarChart for categories and a few periods; use Sparkline when only the shape matters.
components.behavior: Charts measure their container. Keyboard focus reads each point; the Table button lists every value. Keep series in a stable order so colours stay meaningful.

components.name: BarChart
components.title: Bar chart
components.useWhen: People compare values across categories or a few periods, grouped or stacked.
components.inContext: An orders tile compares twelve months with the busiest month highlighted.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use BarList for ranked lists with long labels; use LineChart for many periods.
components.behavior: Highlight one bar only when it answers the tile title. Values can be shown on the bars; the table view lists them all.

components.name: DonutChart
components.title: Donut chart
components.useWhen: A total splits into two to six parts and the share of each part matters.
components.inContext: A revenue tile splits the total by sales channel with a legend beside the ring.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use ProportionBar for a compact split under a figure; use BarChart when parts must be compared precisely.
components.behavior: Order segments meaningfully and keep that order stable. The legend carries values for screen readers.

components.name: BarList
components.title: Bar list
components.useWhen: A ranked list of items with values, such as top pages or low stock.
components.inContext: A low stock tile lists products with the days of stock left, each linking to the product.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Table when rows need several columns or actions.
components.behavior: Rows with href are links. Keep labels short enough to read inside the bar.

components.name: Gauge
components.title: Gauge
components.useWhen: One part of a whole needs emphasis, such as seats used or a plan share.
components.inContext: A customers tile shows the share on the Team plan as a half ring with the other plans in the legend.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use ProportionBar or DonutChart when all parts matter equally.
components.behavior: Keep to one headline share. The legend lists every part with its value.

components.name: ProportionBar
components.title: Proportion bar
components.useWhen: A compact split of two to six parts, often under a figure.
components.inContext: A satisfaction tile shows the average rating, then how reviews split from Excellent to Poor.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use DonutChart when the split is the headline.
components.behavior: Shares print above their parts; the legend carries the values for screen readers.

components.name: Heatmap
components.title: Heatmap
components.useWhen: Peaks across two categories matter, such as weekday by hour or weekday by month.
components.inContext: A busiest-days tile shows average daily orders by weekday and month; compact density fits twelve months in half a row.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use BarChart for exact comparisons. Keep rows and columns in natural order rather than sorting by value.
components.behavior: Darker means more on one hue. Arrow keys move between cells and each cell is announced with its row, column and value; the table view lists every value.

components.name: Tile
components.title: Tile
components.useWhen: A dashboard needs one idea per box: a figure, a chart or a short list.
components.inContext: A dashboard bento grid mixes surface tiles with a few coloured ones for the figures that matter most.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Panel for forms and settings. Keep one structure in every tile: label, description, then content.
components.behavior: Tones re-point the colour tokens so content inside stays readable. Use colour sparingly: a few coloured tiles guide the eye, many cancel each other out.

components.name: Figure
components.title: Figure
components.useWhen: A headline number with its caption and change sits inside a tile.
components.inContext: An orders tile shows 1,285 with an up 4.1% chip and the caption Placed, vs previous 30 days.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use StatCard for a standalone card. Keep to two figure sizes on a page.
components.behavior: Say what the number counts and over which period. Changes pair an arrow with words.

components.name: TabBar
components.title: Tab bar
components.useWhen: A phone app has three to five top-level destinations that people switch between often.
components.inContext: A booking app keeps Home, Explore, Bookings, Saved and Profile in a bar fixed to the bottom of the screen.
components.chooseAndCompose: Use Tabs for views within one page and NavigationList for a sidebar on larger screens. Keep labels to one short word and give every item an icon.
components.behavior: The application owns the current destination and routing. Badges show counts that matter, not decoration. Keep the bar above the safe area on phones.

blocks.name: AppShell
blocks.title: App shell
blocks.useWhen: An application needs a persistent frame: sidebar navigation, a top bar with search and actions, and a menu drawer on small screens.
blocks.inContext: An admin application keeps its sidebar sticky on desktop; below 960 pixels the same navigation opens from a menu button.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Put brand, navigation and account in the sidebar and page actions in PageHeader. Use SidebarPanel inside the shell when the sidebar also lists projects.
blocks.behavior: Render one shell per page. The drawer traps focus and returns it to the menu button; the application closes it after navigation and owns routes.

blocks.name: PageHeader
blocks.title: Page header
blocks.useWhen: An application page needs its title with breadcrumbs, a short description, status and page actions.
blocks.inContext: A customer page shows the path back to Customers, the customer name, an Active tag and an Edit action.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use WorkspaceHeader when the header also searches the section. Keep one primary action.
blocks.behavior: Keep headingLevel 1 on a real page. Actions wrap below the title on narrow screens.

examples.title: Breadcrumbs and actions
A record with status

blocks.name: SidebarPanel
blocks.title: Sidebar panel
blocks.useWhen: A workspace needs a persistent navigation structure with a primary creation action, project access, and account controls.
blocks.inContext: A campaign workspace places its main destinations above pinned and recent projects. Each project's menu offers actions affecting that project, while account controls remain clearly separate.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Keep navigation destinations predictable and project actions contextual. Use the existing Drawer composition for narrow layouts when navigation cannot remain visible. Avoid adding unrelated status messages or dense form controls to the sidebar.
blocks.behavior: The application owns routes, active destination, permissions, pinning, deletion, and account actions. Preserve discoverability when lists grow and give ambiguous project names enough context. Destructive project actions must identify the affected project.

examples.title: Projects and account
No projects yet

blocks.name: PromptInput
blocks.title: AI prompt input
blocks.useWhen: A user submits a written instruction, optionally with files, to start a generation or assistance task.
blocks.inContext: A campaign assistant accepts a request and a brief document, shows the attachment near the editor, and keeps the send action easy to find.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use TextArea for ordinary form prose and AttachmentArea when a custom note composer is needed. Keep optional attachment controls subordinate to the writing task. Place selected attachments above the action row.
blocks.behavior: Keep the draft and attachments available if sending fails. Make busy, disabled, and read-only states reflect the real workflow. Ctrl/Cmd+Enter is an additional send path; keep the visible action. The application performs uploads and generation, handles results, and decides when the composer clears.

examples.title: With an attachment
Send failed

blocks.name: CodeExample
blocks.title: Code example
blocks.useWhen: Documentation needs a live preview, its exact source, and an action to copy that source.
blocks.inContext: A Vertical Stepper page has one base Overview and distinct Examples for headers only and descriptions. Each example copies the variant shown in its own preview.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Give each meaningful variant its own panel. A preview should illustrate one understandable pattern; move unrelated components to their own pages. Use code-only presentation for installation instructions.
blocks.behavior: Keep source and preview consistent, include necessary imports and state in usable examples, and describe any surrounding application responsibilities. Copy must return the exact intended variant. Use a meaningful filename and heading hierarchy. A successful copy means clipboard completion, not that the pasted component has been integrated into an application.

blocks.name: WorkspaceHeader
blocks.title: Workspace header
blocks.useWhen: A workspace page needs a section introduction, optional search and a small set of related actions.
blocks.inContext: A specimen archive names the current collection and lets people search by place while adding a record.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use the optional search field when filtering the content shown in the section. Keep actions specific to that content and let them wrap at narrow widths.
blocks.behavior: The application owns search state, filtering and action effects. Use the heading level that fits the surrounding page hierarchy.

examples.title: With actions
With search

blocks.name: WorkspaceSwitcher
blocks.title: Workspace switcher
blocks.useWhen: People need to change the current workspace or collection without losing the broader application context.
blocks.inContext: A research group switches between a personal field notebook and shared reference collections.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use the menu for a short list. Choose searchable mode when groups, descriptions or a longer collection list make scanning difficult. Mark unavailable choices disabled and keep their reason available elsewhere when it matters.
blocks.behavior: The value is controlled by the application. Update it in response to `onChange`; a chosen ID does not change the trigger until the parent supplies the new value. If the ID is missing, the supplied label remains visible and no other workspace is selected implicitly. The application owns permissions and navigation.

examples.title: Menu
Searchable groups

blocks.name: AccountMenu
blocks.title: Account menu
blocks.useWhen: A user needs access to personal destinations or commands from a consistent identity control.
blocks.inContext: A collection editor can open a profile, adjust reading preferences or see the organization associated with the account.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use menu links for destinations and commands for actions that run in place. Keep organization information as context rather than presenting it as an action.
blocks.behavior: The application owns destination URLs, account data, authorization and command effects. Give each command a distinct label and identify the target clearly for any consequential operation.

examples.title: Personal account
With organization

blocks.name: PrimaryNavigation
blocks.title: Primary navigation
blocks.useWhen: A persistent rail needs to connect the product's main destinations with an optional brand link and supporting footer content.
blocks.inContext: A field archive lists overview, specimen records and preferences, while a review action stays available below those destinations.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use the shared NavigationList items for links, current destination, nested groups and compact presentation. Keep footer content secondary to route navigation and use responsive application layout for a mobile drawer.
blocks.behavior: The block does not create a drawer or decide routes. The application supplies the navigation label, route destinations, active item, mobile behavior and footer interactions. Preserve consistent destination order between compact and expanded presentations.

examples.title: Expanded rail
Compact rail

blocks.name: BreadcrumbHeader
blocks.title: Breadcrumb header
blocks.useWhen: A detail page needs its location within a hierarchy, a clear page title and optional page actions.
blocks.inContext: A shoreline record shows its collection and survey ancestors above the current record title.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Link earlier breadcrumb entries to real destinations; keep the current page nonlinked. Supply a save callback only when users can edit the title, and include actions only when they apply to the page itself.
blocks.behavior: InlineText owns its editing, rejected-save feedback and draft preservation. The application validates and persists accepted changes and supplies route links. Use a concise current title that remains understandable outside its breadcrumb trail.

examples.title: Static title
Editable title

blocks.name: CommandSearch
blocks.title: Command search
blocks.useWhen: A command dialog should also help users reopen a small set of recent destinations.
blocks.inContext: An archive search groups available actions separately from recently opened observation records; choosing an action runs it, while choosing a record navigates to its supplied `href`.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use CommandMenu for one homogeneous result collection, and CommandSearch when commands and recent destinations need distinct outcomes. Keep primary navigation and important actions available in the surrounding interface.
blocks.behavior: CommandSearch delegates modal behavior, filtering, focus, keyboard interaction and optional shortcut handling to CommandMenu. Provide unique IDs within each input collection; matching command and destination IDs are allowed. The application owns command effects, destination URLs and recent-item policy.

examples.title: Commands with a shortcut
Commands and recent destinations

blocks.name: SignInPanel
blocks.title: Sign-in panel
blocks.useWhen: A product needs one controlled entry point for password sign-in or an email-link request.
blocks.inContext: A field archive keeps email and password fields together, offers an email-link alternative, and links to recovery and registration routes.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use password mode when the application supports credential entry. Use email-link mode when the application initiates a link request; this mode removes the password field and submits an empty password even if the controlled value retains an earlier password. Optional provider actions are independent application integrations.
blocks.behavior: The consuming application owns credential checks, provider calls, sessions, route changes and field errors. Keep controlled values after failure, report pending state to block repeated submission, and describe simulation examples as local-only.

examples.title: Password
Email link

blocks.name: RegistrationPanel
blocks.title: Registration panel
blocks.useWhen: People need to create an account with an application-defined set of required identity details and consent.
blocks.inContext: A reader creates a field archive profile with name, email, password and an explicit terms choice. An invited collaborator sees the address and workspace attached to the invitation.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Supply PasswordRequirement entries whose met values are computed by the application. In invitation mode, show the invitation email read-only and ensure the controlled email still matches it. Add only consent the application actually requires.
blocks.behavior: Native required and email constraints support basic form validation. The application owns password policy, consent records, persistence, invitation authorization and all async outcomes. A visible requirement list communicates supplied results; it does not establish a hidden password policy.

examples.title: Open registration
Invitation

blocks.name: RecoveryPanel
blocks.title: Recovery panel
blocks.useWhen: A user needs to request account recovery through an application-owned delivery flow.
blocks.inContext: A reader enters an email address and receives a neutral confirmation with a deliberate option to request another link.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Show the request form before submission and the supplied completion state afterward. Set `retryHref` to the application-owned recovery request route when another request is available; the panel renders it as a link.
blocks.behavior: Supply neutral success copy that does not reveal whether an account exists. The application owns request delivery, rate limits, navigation and outcomes; the panel has no auth service or cooldown timer. Failed requests keep the controlled email available for recovery.

examples.title: Request
Request sent

blocks.name: VerificationPanel
blocks.title: Verification panel
blocks.useWhen: An application requires a one-time numeric code to confirm an address or continue a task.
blocks.inContext: A reader enters a six-digit code sent to the address shown in the panel and can request another when the application allows it.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Set the digit count to the code format and optionally set `name` when the form needs one concatenated code field. Use the supplied resend availability and message to explain when another code can be requested. Keep expired and pending state tied to the actual application response.
blocks.behavior: DigitInput presents a labelled native input per digit, advances focus as digits are entered and distributes pasted codes while retaining a single controlled string value. The application verifies the code, decides expiry and controls resend availability. Do not add an independent cooldown or claim that a code was verified before the application confirms it.

examples.title: Enter code
Expired code

blocks.name: ProfileSummary
blocks.title: Profile summary
blocks.useWhen: A person or organization needs a concise identity card with selected facts and optional actions.
blocks.inContext: A research directory shows a field editor's role and contact details, while a collection page identifies the organization that owns a shared archive.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Set `kind` to distinguish a person from an organization. Supply only the facts useful in this context, and use actions for specific caller-owned tasks. Use AccountMenu for a compact identity control with destinations and commands.
blocks.behavior: The application supplies identity, image, details, and actions. Avatar displays initials when an image cannot load; it does not resolve or store an image. Avoid disclosing contact or membership details that the current audience should not see.

examples.title: Person
Organization

blocks.name: ProfileSettings
blocks.title: Profile settings
blocks.useWhen: People can review or edit their name, email, description, and optionally request a profile image change.
blocks.inContext: A field editor updates their directory details and selects a new portrait while the workspace application handles persistence.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Provide controlled values and update them from `onChange`. Use `readOnly` when details should remain visible without editing. Add avatar selection only when the application accepts files and can supply upload progress or results.
blocks.behavior: The block does not infer saved values or perform saves and uploads. The application owns validation, field errors, authorization, upload limits, outcome state, and recovery. FileDropzone applies its configured local checks before the parent receives selected files; only show successful completion after the upload succeeds.

examples.title: Details
With photo upload

blocks.name: PreferencesPanel
blocks.title: Preferences panel
blocks.useWhen: Several related settings need one save point, such as notification choices or appearance options.
blocks.inContext: A workspace settings page groups email updates, activity digests, and display preferences under named sections.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Pass shared fields such as Checkbox, RadioGroup, Toggle, ColorPicker, and TextField through each section's content slot. Use a standalone form when there is only one field group; use Tabs only when users need to move between substantial independent settings pages.
blocks.behavior: The application owns field values, validation, persistence, and cancellation. Pending state disables the sections. Read-only mode omits save actions; supply readOnly on text fields when users should still copy their values.

examples.title: Notifications
Appearance

blocks.name: MemberDirectory
blocks.title: Member directory
blocks.useWhen: People need to identify workspace members and their contact details or roles.
blocks.inContext: A compact list supports browsing a small collection team; a table supports scanning and selecting members for a batch operation.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use list layout for identity-focused browsing and table layout for repeated comparisons or controlled selection. A simple AvatarGroup is a summary, not a directory. Supply Menu actions only for commands supported by the consuming application.
blocks.behavior: The supplied member array is authoritative. Selection is enabled only when selectedIds and onSelectionChange are both provided, and disabled members are unavailable for selection. The application owns invitations, removals, role changes, filtering, permissions, and data loading. Error and retry callbacks report state without mutating it.

examples.title: List
Selectable table

blocks.name: AccessPanel
blocks.title: Access panel
blocks.useWhen: A user needs to review or edit a role and the permissions associated with one resource.
blocks.inContext: A collection owner selects Reader, Editor, or Owner, then chooses additional permission options for a particular collection.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use RadioCardGroup for role choices that benefit from descriptions and CheckboxCard for longer permission explanations. Use MemberDirectory when the task is to manage a set of people rather than one access policy.
blocks.behavior: The application owns authorization, role-to-permission policy, submission, and persistence. Role changes report a new role ID while retaining the supplied permission IDs; no policy is inferred. Disabled permissions can include a visible reason, but UI state does not enforce backend access. Submission failures preserve the controlled selection for correction and retry.

examples.title: Role only
Role and permissions

blocks.name: SiteHeader
blocks.title: Site header
blocks.useWhen: The top of a public website or marketing page needs the brand, a handful of main pages and one or two actions such as signing in or starting a trial.
blocks.inContext: A notes app’s website links Product, Pricing and Docs, with Sign in and a primary Start free button; on phones they open from a menu button.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use AppShell or PrimaryNavigation for application frames with a persistent rail, and PageHeader for the title row of a page.
blocks.behavior: The application supplies real links, marks the current page, handles routing and decides whether the header sticks to the top. The block only keeps the drawer’s open state.

examples.title: Compact links
Grouped navigation

blocks.name: ReleaseNotice
blocks.title: Release notice
blocks.useWhen: A website needs to announce something time-sensitive, such as a new release or an early-access offer.
blocks.inContext: A landing page shows “Pro is open to the waitlist” with a link to pricing and a close control.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use Banner for workspace conditions such as maintenance, Alert for problems inside a task and Toast for brief feedback. Show one notice at a time.
blocks.behavior: The application decides whether it can be dismissed, removes it when onDismiss fires, remembers the dismissal and decides when a newer notice replaces it.

blocks.name: IntroSection
blocks.title: Intro section
blocks.useWhen: A page or a major area of a website opens by saying what it is about.
blocks.inContext: A product page says what the product does in one sentence, offers Start free and a secondary tour link, and shows an animated illustration beside the copy.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use PageHeader for application pages with breadcrumbs, SectionHeading for headings further down, and ActionSection for a closing call to action.
blocks.behavior: The application owns the heading level (one h1 per page), the actions and the media, including its accessible name and loading.

blocks.name: CapabilityGrid
blocks.title: Capability grid
blocks.useWhen: A website explains a set of concrete features, each worth a name and a sentence.
blocks.inContext: A pricing page lists what every plan includes: templates, components, dark theme, accessibility.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use ProcessSteps when order matters and DescriptionList for label and value facts.
blocks.behavior: The application owns the copy, links, media and the order of items.

blocks.name: ProcessSteps

blocks.inContext: A landing page shows install, connect your assistant, ask for a screen.

blocks.name: PlanComparison
blocks.title: Plan comparison
blocks.useWhen: A pricing page compares two to four plans of one service.
blocks.inContext: A product offers a free plan and two paid plans with a monthly or yearly switch; the recommended plan is marked.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: A single offer belongs in ActionSection; a one-off choice inside a form belongs in RadioCardGroup.
blocks.behavior: The application owns price formatting, currency, tax wording, the selected period, checkout destinations and any discount claims.

blocks.name: SubscriptionSection
blocks.title: Subscription section
blocks.useWhen: A website invites readers to join a mailing list or a waitlist.
blocks.inContext: A landing page ends its pricing section with a waitlist form that explains what people will receive.
blocks.chooseAndCompose: Use a composed Form when you need several fields or separate consents.
blocks.behavior: The block sends nothing. The application owns the request, validation beyond the native checks, consent records, rate limiting and the success message.
